items_missed: The customer's name was never asked for and never captured. The transcript speaker is '(469) 243-7314' from the first line to the last — through a full quote, a scheduling negotiation, two unit numbers and a confirmed booking. He booked a move without ever learning who he booked it for.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or ran any warm-up.
No agenda statement. 'Well, let me get a few more details from you' is the entire roadmap — no sequence, no timeframe, no 'sound good?'

Additional rooms never probed — no garage contents, no patio, no storage closet. The customer explicitly mentioned an attached garage on the first floor and Jules never asked whether anything in it is moving.

Special considerations never asked — no long walks, no narrow hallways, no tight turns. Worse, the customer volunteered the one access complication on the call — 'I think you have to get around to the other side to get to the front of the apartment' — and Jules waved it off: 'Got it. No problem. That's totally fine.' He dismissed the only access red flag he was handed, on a move he then priced at the bare minimum.
Packing needs never asked and packing service never offered. The customer said 'I don't have everything packed yet' — an unprompted buying signal for a paid service — and it drew no response at all.
Additional stops never asked.
Access never probed — no parking, no elevator, no gate, no loading area, at either end.
Moving-stressor question never asked.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener.
Packing service pricing never given, on a customer who said out loud he is not packed.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. 'Insurance' appears once, inside the inclusions list. No $2,000, no repair/replace/reimburse, no brand name, no 60-cents-per-pound baseline — on a booked job moving two couches and a TV down a flight of stairs.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — and this is the costliest miss on the call, because he created the exact problem it solves. He told the customer 'right now we cannot guarantee exactly the time we would be arriving because we usually have a move scheduled in the morning,' handed over a two-hour window, and attached no promise to it. The guarantee exists precisely to turn that sentence from a warning into a differentiator.
Clock start never explained — nothing about the clock starting on-site when the contract opens.

No typical time range for this home size was ever given. He went straight to a point commitment — 'I think yeah, this we would just be within the minimum of two and a half hours' — with no band around it, so the customer has heard $510 as a price, not as a floor.
Stairs never factored into the estimate. He confirmed first floor to second floor and then quoted as if the move were flat.
Specialty items never probed. A TV was on the inventory list and he never asked the size, never asked if it is wall-mounted, never asked if there is a box for it.
Drive time never discussed. 3700 Legacy Drive to 8404 Barron Parkway is a real cross-Plano run and the customer was never told whether it is on the clock.
Walk distance never asked, on the one point the customer specifically raised.
Traffic never mentioned. Packing time never factored despite an unpacked customer. No equivalents used anywhere.
Save Your Ass entirely absent — 0/10, on a partial-move customer who is not packed, is cost-focused enough to do the price math out loud, and was booked at the minimum.
No deposit required was never mentioned.

BOLDED-details framing absent and the 'reply with any corrections' verification ask absent. He collected two unit numbers by ear — '5102' and '0726' — plus two street addresses, and never read any of it back or asked the customer to check the confirmation email. On a move that is now on the schedule, a transposed unit number is a crew standing in the wrong parking lot.
Hours and how to reach us never given.

The arrival window was stated twice as '12:30 AM to 2:30 PM,' which is not a window. Whether that is a transcription artifact or what the customer actually heard, it was said twice and never clarified.
Customer's name used zero times — he never had it.
top_strength: Jules is fast, and on the commercial mechanics he is genuinely good. The best moment on the call is the availability handling, which is where most reps lose a date and he saved one. The customer wanted the twenty-fifth; Jules did not have it, and instead of stalling or offering to check, he came back inside one sentence with the alternative and then immediately made it concrete: 'Unfortunately, we are fully booked on the twenty fifth but we do have available either the day before or the day after.' When the customer asked what times, he had them ready — morning around 8:30 to nine, or the afternoon slot — and the customer said 'Okay, I can do that' within seconds. A no turned into a yes in about twenty seconds because he led with the alternatives rather than the problem. He then volunteered the day-of-week savings without being asked, which is a small thing almost nobody does: 'we can certainly help you out on that Thursday. The hour rate for Thursday is actually cheaper than Friday.' That is the rep pointing out that the customer's forced compromise is also cheaper — good instinct, and it framed the schedule change as a win rather than a concession. The second real strength is how he handled the customer's pricing error, which is a moment that easily goes wrong. The customer worked the math out loud and got it wrong — 'so it'll be basically $400' — and Jules corrected without a trace of condescension: 'Well, the minimum of two and a half hours is $510.' The customer pushed back ('Is it, but you said it's $204 per hour'), and Jules held it simply: 'Yes, and the minimum is two and a half hours, not two.' The customer's response was 'Okay, okay, sorry I missed the half,' and Jules immediately took the sting out with 'No problem.' A price correction that ends with the customer apologizing and still booking is well handled. He also did real proactive expectation-setting on arrival, flagging the window caveat before the customer could be surprised by it, and telling them about the day-of call: 'the guys will also give you a call on the day of to give you a more accurate ETA. They're gonna give you a call half an hour before they arrive.' And he is the only rep in this batch besides Nicole Cruz to describe the Meet Your Mover email at all: 'The next email you'd received from us is gonna be a few days before your move to introduce you to your movers.'
coaching_note: Estimate-accuracy flag, and this is the sharpest one in the batch — it goes in the bottom-4 review file. Jules booked this move at the bare 2.5-hour minimum, $510, for two couches, a dresser, a bed, a TV and a round table, moving from a first-floor attached garage up to a second-floor apartment, across town from Legacy Drive to Barron Parkway, for a customer who said he is not packed. He gave no range at all — just 'I think yeah, this we would just be within the minimum of two and a half hours.' Two couches up a flight of stairs is routinely an hour by itself; add the drive, the TV and the bed disassembly and this is a three-to-four-hour job. He also dismissed the only access warning he was given: the customer said 'you have to get around to the other side to get to the front of the apartment' and got 'Got it. No problem. That's totally fine.' This is the apartment-underestimate half of the pattern Amanda's rock names — the flip side of managers padding large homes — and it is worth pulling the actual on this job when it runs, because if it lands at three and a half hours the customer was quoted $510 and will be billed closer to $715. That is a $200 surprise on a customer who did the math out loud because money matters to him, and it is exactly how a booked move becomes a Daniel Behseresht refund call. The fix is one sentence of structure that costs ten seconds: state the benchmark, then adjust with named reasons, then give a range. 'For a one-bedroom partial like this we typically see two and a half to three and a half hours. With the stairs at your new place and the drive between the two, I'd budget three to three and a half — call it $610 to $715 — and remember we only bill for the time we actually use, so if we come in at the minimum you pay the minimum.' Second priority: the Save Your Ass speech is a zero and it is the direct antidote to the problem above. This customer is not packed, is moving only big furniture, and is price-sensitive. 'Here's how you keep this at the minimum — anything you can carry, take a carload or two over before Thursday. Loose stuff out of the drawers, closet odds and ends, the small kitchen things, pictures off the walls. Every load you take yourself comes straight off the clock.' That both lowers the real hours and protects the quote, which is the whole point of the section. Third: he booked a move for an anonymous phone number. No first name, no last name, no email confirmation read back, and two unit numbers taken by ear with no verification. The record for this job is a phone number and two digit strings. Get the name in the first thirty seconds and read the email and unit numbers back before ending the call — 'I've got unit 5102 at Legacy and 0726 at Barron, and I'll send the confirmation now with all of it bolded at the top. Have a quick look and reply with any corrections.' That closes three missing bullets at once. Fourth, the On-Time Guarantee. He told the customer we cannot guarantee the arrival time and then left it there. That is the single worst place in the batch to omit it. The sentence he needed was: 'and if we miss that window, we start discounting your bill immediately.' Last, confirm what window was actually given — '12:30 AM to 2:30 PM' was stated twice and is not a real window.
phone_presence_notes: Efficient and unflappable — he turned a fully-booked date into a confirmed Thursday in under a minute and corrected the customer's price math without making him feel stupid ('No problem') — but the warmth is thin and repetitive, with 'Got it.' appearing five times as the primary acknowledgment, no name ever captured or used, no warm-up, and no moment of rapport across the whole 5.4 minutes.
audio_review_reason: Two things need ears on them. First, the arrival window is transcribed as '12:30 AM to 2:30 PM' twice — audio is the only way to confirm whether the customer was actually handed a coherent window on a move that is now on the schedule, or whether Jules misspoke it and nobody caught it. Second, the score is a 3 driven largely by the clipped register — five flat 'Got it's and no warm-up — and that is exactly the pattern text renders badly. A rep who sounds brisk and confident and a rep who sounds like he is rushing the customer off the phone produce nearly identical transcripts, and the coaching is opposite in each case. Given the call booked in 5.4 minutes, it is worth knowing which one this was before telling him to slow down.
